Do you take a lot of notes? Whether it's daily to-do lists, notes for class, or just jotting down thoughts, I've found the best digital notebooks to keep them organized. Sure, you could just open your Notes app , but physically writing something down helps you remember and learn more. Plus, I just love to write things down, and these digital notebooks keep me from burning through paper or losing a great idea I wrote down.
Most of these tablets use E Ink technology to give you a more paperlike experience to write your ideas and notes on. It's easy on the eyes and helps keep you distraction-free as you take your notes as a classic notebook would. As our team's resident obsessive notetaker, I've tried almost every digital notebook on the market to find the best ones worth buying. Whether you want to be able to take detailed notes and access them on your laptop, annotate a book, or have near-never-ending battery life, I've found a digital notebook for you. They're especially great for students who need to do a lot of note-taking and stay engaged without getting distracted by notifications and other apps.
If your notes need an upgrade, I highly recommend giving these a try. If you're looking for more organizational tools and e-paper gadgets, don't miss my guides to the Best Paper Planners , Best Digital Wall Calendars , and Best E-Readers That Aren't a Kindle .
Updated November 2026: The Supernote Manta is now our runner-up pick, and the Supernote Nomad is now our budget pick.
The ReMarkable Paper Pro has everything we like about the ReMarkable 2—a matte screen feels like paper, quick and responsive writing experience, and a great battery life—and adds a few cool new features like colorful pen options and a gentle built-in screen light that uses ambient light from the room. It's got an 11.8-inch screen, making it an extra inch and a half bigger than the ReMarkable 2. It's especially handy if you're taking notes or writing down ideas somewhere a little dark, like a dimmed classroom or on a late flight. Like the ReMarkable 2, it's easy to organize your notes in various ways, from different notebooks to tags and folders. It's easy to access notes off the device, too, especially if you have ReMarkable's Connect subscription ($4 per month) for unlimited cloud storage. The stylus charges on the device, too.
There are many ways to organize your work into different notebooks or quick sheets, and you can sort them with tags and folders. You also upload PDFs and ebooks to the slate via the company's app or website, and ReMarkable has a Chrome extension that lets you send any webpage to read on the tablet, and a desktop app that lets you upload PDFs, like a blank Dungeons & Dragons character sheet to fill in on your next game night. You can integrate your notes into Google Drive, Dropbox, or Microsoft OneDrive, though you'll want the Connect subscription for unlimited cloud storage. You can also join the beta program for ReMarkable Methods as a Connect subscriber, which introduces a new library of templates and workbooks you can add to your ReMarkable device. There's also a beta program (that again you'll need to be a subscriber to join) for the new Handwriting Search, which will scan your notes to learn what you've written and allow you to search for it.
The Paper Pro does have its own set of accessories, including covers ($179) to protect it and a keyboard folio ($229) if you want to type with it, since it's a different size than the ReMarkable 2. It has its own set of styluses as well, the Marker and Marker Plus—the Marker Plus is a $50 upgrade, but I find the eraser to be well worth it.
The Supernote Manta is the second generation of Supernote's A5 digital notebook, and it's a great option with new upgrades like a dual slider bar, upgraded RAM, and FeelWrite 2 film covering the screen to give it a feeling similar to paper. You can also expand the storage with a microSD card, and there's a modular design under the hood so that you can easily upgrade the motherboard or put in a new battery.
The software is easy to use and has a design similar to ReMarkable’s, with plenty of templates to choose from for your notes. There’s also a cloud website and app you can use to send PDFs to the digital notebook to edit, and you can also integrate it with apps like Google Drive and Dropbox. You can also add on the app Atelier to get a digital sketchbook option (though it's only in shades of grayscale), which I found fun and easy to use for a little drawing. Supernote will also convert your handwriting into a typed document, but you'll need to select that type of document from the beginning rather than just use a tool to convert any handwriting in any file.
But where Supernote really shines is that it has, in my opinion, the best pens in the game. My favorite is the clear LAMY Safari Vista EMR ($99) pen that looks so realistic, I keep grabbing it to write in my paper planner, but it's currently out of stock. However, there's still the Heart of Metal ($83) pen that also has an impressively realistic feel to it, with a little more weight to it thanks to the metal body. Ultimately, if you're a bit of a pen and stationery nerd (and don't need a keyboard attachment, which Supernote doesn't offer), then you'll get your heart's fill with Supernote's pen lineup paired with its great digital notebook.
This is a smaller version of the Supernote Manta , measuring almost 6 inches on one side and 7.5 inches on the other. Supernote designed it with travel in mind, but I find it to be a great size for a daily digital to-do list or writing down quick notes from a meeting. It's a good size to stack on top of other notebooks or slide into a variety of bags with its smaller size.
It's too small for anything major, though it's not as small as the reMarkable Paper Pro Move , which has a slim reporter's notebook-style design. The Supernote Nomad has a more similar size and feel to an e-reader, which is great if you're not looking for something large to tote around. It's also a good price point, though once you add on the pen it'll cost a little more than the older Kindle Scribe and reMarkable Move, so you can buy those if you want to spend the least amount possible to get a device. You'll get a larger screen with the Supernote Nomad, but the reMarkable Paper Pro Move has a color screen if you'd rather prioritize that with your budget. Supernote also designed this digital notebook with repairability in mind like the Manta, and has guides on its website to allow you to replace the battery, motherboard, and microSD card.
Kobo makes some of our favorite e-readers , and the Kobo Libra Colour takes its e-reader software and not only adds digital notebooks, but color annotating, too. You can write in the margins and underline your favorite quotes using eight different colors (plus black and gray, giving you 10 choices total), and you can hold down the button on the Stylus 2 ($70) to enter highlight mode. You can only highlight books in yellow, but there are four highlighter colors in notebook mode. The Stylus 2 also has an eraser on the back that works as an object eraser, so one tap to the highlighted area or on-page doodle and the whole thing will vanish from your book's page.
The Libra also has a separate notebook section, where you can create different digital notebook pages. You can choose from a variety of layouts for each page (click the three dots and choose “change page background”) in a notebook, plus three different pen styles, a highlighter, and a paintbrush to use with the eight colors and two neutrals in the Libra's digital palette. It is a small size, so good for taking quick notes but not ideal for, say, writing down everything from an intense lecture. My handwriting also didn't appear as clearly as it did on ReMarkable and Scribe devices. But if you're more of a quick-list or idea kind of person and mainly want to annotate your e-books with color, the Kobo Libra Colour will be perfect for…

Spain, who are unbeaten in their last 43 competitive meetings, host England in Madrid on Sunday.
Who : Spain vs England What : UEFA Nations League, Group A3 Where : Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid, Spain When : Sunday, November 15, at 7:45pm (19:45 GMT). How to follow : Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream.
England have the chance to avenge their defeat and end Spain’s 43-match unbeaten record when they face the reigning world champions in Sunday’s final Nations League group encounter.
Spain staged a 3-2 comeback victory at London’s Wembley Stadium in late September, as Lamine Yamal scored an early opener and Mikel Oyarzabal finished the job.
Spain and England have both sealed their berth in the competition’s quaterfinals, with La Roja assured of the top spot should they avoid defeat on Sunday. England, meanwhile, will finish second if they fail to beat the two-time World Cup winners.
Teenage sensation Yamal, with four goals, and Mikel Merino, with three, have headlined Spain’s attacking charge, while newly-crowned Ballon d’Or recipient Harry Kane leads England.
Before Spain vs England, here’s everything you need to know:
Spain have a perfect record and lead Group A3 with 15 points.
They beat England 3-2 in the first game, an away trip, and followed it with a 4-1 rout of Croatia at home.
Then, they beat Czechia 3-1 at home, followed by a 2-1 away win over Croatia and a 2-0 away win over Czechia.
England are second in Group A3 with 12 points from five games, having won four times and lost once.
Their Nations League campaign started with a 3-2 home defeat to Spain before Thomas Tuchel’s side beat Czechia 2-0 and thrashed Croatia 7-0 in back-to-back away fixtures.
Tuchel believes England are ready to end Spain’s unbeaten record when they face the world and European champions in Madrid.
While victory offers little more than the prospect of a more favourable Nations League quarterfinal in March, it would be a landmark moment for England if they could end Spain’s run of 43 matches without defeat.
“It (Spain) is a team that has forgotten how to lose, so of course it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost,” said Tuchel.
“I think we’re there, and I think we’re ready to win on Sunday.
“I know what it takes, and no one can ever guarantee it, but I think it’s the moment to check how far we are and to push our limit and proof of concept,” the German added.
“It’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength.”
De la Fuente said their unbeaten record provided his players with extra motivation.
“We want to keep setting new milestones, and this is another one,” he explained.
“None of us would probably ever have thought we’d even reach 35, because we already felt those were astronomical numbers, but having reached 43, you think, my goodness, we want to get to 44, of course we do.”
Spain came from behind to beat England 3-2 in an entertaining Nations League encounter on September 26, denying the hosts a cathartic win after their painful World Cup exit.
Yamal put Spain ahead in the second minute, but Anthony Gordon equalised, and Kane added another as England ended the first half with a 2-1 lead.
The Three Lions captain missed a penalty in the second half, though, allowing Spain to bounce back, as Alex Baena found the equaliser before Oyarzabal sealed victory in the 74th minute.
Opta’s supercomputer favours Spain for victory. They have a 59.6 percent probability of winning, while England’s odds of victory are 19.3 percent.
Yamal is expected to face England after missing the last game with a knee problem. Nico Williams and Aymeric Laporte are doubtful
Probable Spain XI: Unai Simon; Marc Pubill, Pau Cubarsi, Dean Huijsen, Marc Cucurella; Dani Olmo, Rodri, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Mikel Oyarzabal, Alex Baena
Myles Lewis-Skelly returns from his suspension, while Ezri Konsa is also expected to return after missing the last game due to a knee injury.
Djed Spence (muscle) is doubtful, and Marc Guehi (muscle) remains out with injury.
Probable England XI: Jordan Pickford; Trent Alexander-Arnold, Ezri Konsa, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall; Elliot Anderson, Declan Rice; Morgan Rogers, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon; Harry Kane
You can find your regional broadcaster on UEFA’s official broadcaster listing .

Filipino entry, pop and rap song Sobra-Sobra, takes 19-year-old to victory at grand final in Bangkok
Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra , to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe.
Eleven countries competed at the One Bangkok Forum in central Bangkok, and the show ran for two and a half hours including advertising.
The winner, who performs under the single name Carmelle, finished on 211 points, 41 clear of the hosts Thailand , with Vietnam third. She received the most votes from both the national juries and the public ballot.
Carmelle, 19, grew up beside the railway tracks in the Bicol region of south-eastern Luzon and has been competing in televised talent contests since she was 12.
Sobra-Sobra mixes pop and rap, is supported by traditional Philippine instruments, the kubing and kulintang, and is sung in Tagalog and English.
After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women”.
“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told the Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”
“It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are,” she told the Guardian before the final. “It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas.”
The show opened with a routine celebrating the host country, in which Muay Thai fighters shared the stage with drag performers on street food carts. The 11 acts were then driven on in tuk-tuks, each carrying their national flag.
Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên , a star at home for more than 20 years, performed first, among dancers costumed as lotus leaves. Mang x Daou represented Thailand, a duo assembled for the contest in the host country who performed a duet staged like a musical number.
Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai gave one of the most conventionally Eurovision performances of the night with Ananta Maya , a rock ballad staged with fire imagery and a large heart-shaped structure behind him.
He ended it by appealing for support for his country, which he said was “going [through a] very hard situation”. More than 1,500 people were killed and more than 5,000 were reported missing after a rock and ice avalanche near the Chinese border triggered catastrophic flash floods in August.
Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere , originally a nine-member a cappella and beatbox group, sang without a single instrument. Three of their members were left out of the final due to a rule capping each act at six performers on stage.
Nyendra from Bhutan sang dressed in the gho, his country’s national dress for men, against a backdrop of Himalayan peaks. Mongolia’s Beck performed in a reinterpreted deel, also a national costume.
Half the result was decided before the show began. The 11 national juries voted at a dress rehearsal on Friday night and put the Philippines top with 93 points, ahead of Vietnam and Malaysia.
The other half came from viewers around the world, who could vote online but not for their own country, and who were given eight free votes each and the option to buy 10 more.
Laos’s entrant, Thinla, was unable to hear her own music during her performance, and her dress rehearsal was aired once all live performances were over. She finished fifth, with the night’s third-highest public score.
Carmelle receives no prize money but a trophy presented by Dara, the Bulgarian singer who won this year’s European contest , and will perform at Eurovision 2027 in Burgas.
Organisers have said the right to stage future editions will not automatically go to the winner, on the grounds that smaller countries lack the infrastructure.
Some of the clearest echoes of Eurovision’s camp traditions came through those who announced the votes.
South Korea’s jury points were read by Jo Kwon, a veteran pop star who has played Adam in the Korean production of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and the title role in Everybody’s Talking About Jamie.
The Philippines’ were read by Vice Ganda, a gay comedian who is one of the biggest stars on Philippine television.
Meanwhile, the guest performer was the Thai singer Jeff Satur, who reached a wider Asian audience through KinnPorsche, a 2022 series in the genre of male same-sex romance dramas that has a large following across Asia.
Organisers intend the Bangkok show to be the first of many regional editions, with the executive producer, Assaf Blecher, saying that 16 or 17 territories had expressed interest in competing next year, among them China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.
Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.
She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.
There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.
Carmelle was the youngest contestant in the comeptions at 19 years old
Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.
Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.
Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.
And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.
However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.
Thinla wore a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit during her performance
The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote.
Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.
Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.
Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now.
There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.
Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.
Eurvosion superfans Michael, Scarlett and Zelie travelled from the UK to Thailand to watch Eurovision Asia's first outing
Korea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England.
"The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.
They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.
For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.
However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.
The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday
Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.
The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected.
The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.
Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent.
Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.
Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.
By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.
Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge.
Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected , as were some schools and police forces.
UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network.
In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.
In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.
Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.
In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.
The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.
Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill".
His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".
Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.
"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said.
"We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible."
Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.
It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.
By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.
Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.
Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.
"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.
Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.
"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said .
"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."
Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech

Regulator said Meta’s ‘lack of cooperation’ and the large number of people affected contributed to size of the fine.
Italian regulators have fined Meta 805 million euros ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their consent.
The Facebook app on Android devices “accessed photos, videos and associated metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without specific consent and without informing them”, Garante, the Italian data privacy authority, said Saturday.
The issue relates specifically to the “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from the phone’s gallery for posting while browsing.
This feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said.
Garante said the app’s process for collecting consent is too generic and does not allow users to fully understand the specific permissions they are allowing by accepting. The suggestions option was also enabled by default.
The figure of 805 million euros is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.
Garante said Meta must fix the unclear consent notification and disable it being set by default, suggesting that roughly 20 million Italian Android users could have been affected by it.
The regulator also highlighted a “lack of cooperation” by Meta and said an earlier violation, which resulted in a 2019 fine, was a contributing factor in their decision.
The amount is roughly 0.47 percent of Meta’s global turnover.
The proceedings did not address the possible use of content to train artificial intelligence, which Meta denies.
Meta has not yet publicly commented on the matter, and it has the right to appeal the regulator’s decision.

Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.
Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.
The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law, and the disproportionate level of the fine.
"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate, and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."
Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

A delegation of 18 Democratic lawmakers arrived at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey on Saturday to reaffirm the US commitment to tackling global warming following their sweeping midterm election victory.
Fresh from their US midterm election triumph , an emboldened group of Democratic lawmakers descended on the COP31 climate talks shunned by President Donald Trump on Saturday to signal their commitment to tackling global warming.
The 18-strong delegation joined the annual UN conference in Turkey after their party regained control of both chambers of Congress in a landslide victory last week cheered by climate campaigners.
Read more Why the Democrats routed the Republicans in the US midterm elections
"Many of our allies and partners across the world think the United States has not been predictable or dependable. So we have a lot of trust to earn back," Florida Representative Kathy Castor told AFP.
"We have so much work to do. And yes, I hope the United States gets back on track with urgent climate action," she said after the group took photos in front of a large COP31 sign in a sprawling expo centre.
The election has been a topic of discussion at COP31 in Antalya, with hopes that Democrats can restore some clean energy policies and that a pro-climate president can be elected in two years.
"What happened in the US is remarkable, and a much needed shift that we all needed, not only from a climate perspective, but overall," Harjeet Singh, strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told AFP.
Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has rolled back some of the clean energy policies of his predecessors, promoted oil drilling, pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement and kept his country out of the UN's climate negotiations.
"It is absolutely shameful that the Trump administration operates this way, that this is an administration that is filled with climate deniers, that is beholden to big oil in the United States," Yassamin Ansari, an Arizona lawmaker, told AFP.
Ansari and other members of the delegation spoke at a panel focused on the midterm elections , attracting a crowd that overflowed outside the "America Is All In" pavilion.
The group reminded COP31 delegates that, while Trump has rejected clean energy, US states and local governments have continued to promote renewables and other pro-climate policies.
A group of US mayors and governors visited COP31 earlier this week, along with former US vice president Al Gore and former US climate envoy and secretary of state John Kerry .
"Despite the setbacks that we're experiencing through this Trump administration, climate action is alive in America," California Congressman Raul Ruiz told the panel.
The president's Republican party was handed a resounding defeat last week in large part due to anger over soaring energy prices and Trump's costly war with Iran .
Democrats have vowed to use their majority in the House and the Senate to launch investigations into the administration's climate policies and propose clean energy legislation.
But Trump still has two years left in office and has vowed to wield his veto power.
"At a time where Americans from all political backgrounds want to see their energy bills reduced, this administration will be very hard pressed to veto legislation that will bring down costs for the American people," Ansari said.

A nuclear treaty and the US’s war on Iran are priority topics for China, Russia, US leaders. But Ukraine is unlikely to be raised.
US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, the White House has confirmed .
On Friday, Washington also confirmed Trump’s attendance at the summit, which will take place from November 18-19.
Talks will focus on nuclear proliferation, the White House said. But they come amid significant global turbulence: Russia’s war in Ukraine, the US-Israeli war on Iran and ongoing trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.
“I think what we’ll see is some pretty impressive photo-ops with a lot of really bombastic rhetoric from Trump,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at the UK’s Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. However, he added, the three “collectively or unilaterally, are not able to bring about an end to the conflict in Iran or Ukraine”.
So what does each side want and what will be the likely outcome?
Each leader has his own priorities, but there are some issues all will want to discuss.
A top issue for Russia and the US is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February. The treaty was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.
Russia currently possesses the largest number of warheads, followed by the US and then China, which is rapidly building up its own arsenal.
Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.
China is understood, however, to be reluctant to join an agreement it was not involved in forming.
A senior Trump administration official told Reuters this topic will start the conversation but that “we do not expect to get any kind of agreement”.
Officials also say the world leaders will discuss the Iran war , which the US and Israel launched on February 28. While full-scale strikes have, for now, ceased, the conflict remains in a deadlock .
After more than 100 days, the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and oil and gas prices are still volatile as ships in the strait continue to face Iranian strikes and seamines. One-third of China’s crude oil supply transited the strait before the war. The conflict is also hampering demand for Chinese exports.
Russia, meanwhile, has profited from rising energy prices and recent sanctions relief from Washington amid supply crunches – particularly of diesel.
Trade wars and the race to control microchips used to power artificial intelligence are straining relations between Beijing and Washington.
Trump hit China with a 145 percent tax hike last year, while Beijing retaliated by imposing 125 percent levies on US imports. Tensions mounted further over China’s restrictions on exports of rare earth minerals needed to manufacture advanced chips and other technology.
The two countries have since reduced tariffs and struck several deals following Trump and Xi’s meetings in South Korea and Washington However, the recent scandal at chip firm Nvidia has prompted the US to allege that China was spying on CEO Jensen Huang. Beijing denies this.
It is very unlikely. A Trump administration official told reporters the US president will not bring up Russia’s war on Ukraine, although Kremlin officials previously suggested the conflict could be discussed.
China, an ally of Moscow’s, has said the Ukraine war is a European issue.
US officials also note that Washington is pursuing peace talks, with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visiting both Ukraine and Russia this week. “China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” an official told reporters.
President Trump has accused Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of “not wanting” to end the war, while Kyiv has reiterated allegations that the US has restricted its Starlink satellite connection that allows it to operate attack drones. Trump has also blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices because of its strikes on Russian oil facilities.
At the same time, Trump has feted Putin, agreed to allow Russian diesel into global and US markets, and lifted oil sanctions on Moscow.
For President Putin, the meeting could provide a positive photo opportunity and a platform to project power while sidelining the Ukraine conflict, analysts say.
It will give him a “first among equals” position that he can display at home to show that he can influence Europe’s security architecture following the Ukraine war, Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Beijing has already been pushing for a resolution to the US war on Iran, which has impacted its own energy supplies.
China will also want to avoid being pulled into a nuclear treaty it had no part in establishing.
Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.
Trump’s priority is to include both China and Russia in a new nuclear proliferation treaty, according to administration officials. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told reporters.
The president could also use the meeting to project his administration’s diplomatic influence, as Iran refuses to capitulate to US demands for ending the war and hand Washington a win.
Trump has also sought closer ties with Xi, Putin and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, all seen as “strongmen”, and is likely to be perceived as influential in such circles, analysts say.
“I think it will be more performative – Donald Trump playing global statesman rather than peacemaker,” said Mabon.
Trump’s Republican Party’s crushing defeat in midterm elections last week could undermine his leverage, experts note, as a new Democrat-led Congress is likely to support Ukraine more staunchly.
Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee said it could lead to a “new Yalta”.
The 1945 conference in Yalta, in the then Soviet Union, saw USSR President Joseph Stalin, the US’s Franklin D Roosevelt, and the United Kingdom’s Winston Churchill divide Germany and establish the United Nations in what was seen as the template for a new world order.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, called the trilateral meeting now taking place between the leaders of the US, China and Russia as “extremely significant” but pointed out that any agreements reached at the meeting cannot be imposed on other nations.

The leaders of the US, Russia and China will meet late next week, according to the White House
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.
The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China , which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.
The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.
Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

US tech giant Microsoft says it has fixed problems that led to a global outage of its services. The glitch severely disrupted online communications in businesses and governments for more than 24 hours.
The US technology conglomerate Microsoft said on Saturday that a more than 24-hour global outage affecting its Microsoft 365 applications used by businesses and governments across the world has now ended.
"We ​have completed our efforts to address ​the underlying issue of the ⁠incident ​and ​restored service to ​the remaining impacted ‌customers and regions," ​the ⁠company posted on X.
Microsoft applications such as Teams, Outlook and Copilot were all hit by the outage, leading to communications problems in scores of countries.
The company has said it was "not aware" of any outside interference that could have been behind the outage, blaming the problem on server issues.
The disruption was one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second this year.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The outage, which began around 1725 UTC on Thursday according to web testing and network diagnostics company ​Ookla, affected government agencies and businesses across much of the world.
It made it impossible to carry out activities such as sending emails and holding online meetings.
Germany was no exception, with a spokesperson for its Federal Ministry for Digital Transformation and Government Modernization saying that while the outage did not have a major impact on federal government functions, it did significantly affect ​German businesses.
Britain's state health service (NHS) was also severely affected, with personnel forced to have recourse to paper records rather than those stored online.
Altogether, there were more than 7.4 million reports of problems worldwide logged by Downdetector, which monitors online outages.
The disruption highlights the widespread and perilous reliance of governments and businesses on a very small number of Big Tech companies.
The problems at Microsoft are so far believed to be unconnected with the major communications outage that has affected US aviation.

Vincent van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs is displayed ahead of this week's auction
Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.
Châtaigniers en Fleurs, which carries an estimate of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.
But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - earlier German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
Sotheby's say its own "extensive research" has not established this, but say they will work with the family to try and reach a solution.
"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," Sotheby's told the BBC in a statement.
"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.
"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."
The painting - whose name translates as Blossoming Chestnut Trees - is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.
Four other owners have had it since before it was put up for auction this year.
Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times , external , has written to Sotherby's.
He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

Appeal for information comes after Brenda Raymond, 80, was set on fire outside her flat on Monday
The family of an elderly woman who was set on fire outside a block of flats in Watford have said that they are “desperate for answers”.
Brenda Raymond, 80, was found set alight outside her flat on Caractacus Cottage View on Monday. She was taken to a nearby hospital, where she is in critical condition.
Hertfordshire constabulary have said that a 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson with intent to endanger life but has been released on bail with strict conditions.
Raymond’s family said the attack had left them in “complete shock” and that they were confused over why she was targeted.
In a statement issued via Hertfordshire constabulary, they said: “Words cannot describe how distressing the past few days have been for us as a family.
“Our beautiful, chatty, fun-loving and much-loved Brenda, who loves to keep fit and dancing, has suffered catastrophic injuries in the most devastating of circumstances; circumstances which have left us all in complete shock.
“We simply cannot understand why anyone would have wanted to hurt her in this way. Someone out there knows something. They know what happened to Brenda. We are desperate for answers and are pleading for anyone with information to please come forward.”
The family also asked for their privacy to be respected during this “unimaginably difficult time”.
Police believe that Raymond was attacked as she returned home at around noon, with her attackers pouring some kind of flammable liquid on her before setting her alight. Detectives said that an accelerant was also poured through the letterbox of a nearby flat, but have not officially linked the two events.
The decision to publicly name Raymond was made by police with the blessing of her family on Wednesday in the hope that it would lead to anyone with knowledge of the attack coming forward.
DI Adam Bridges, from the Major Crime Unit, said: “This was an appalling and deeply distressing attack on an elderly woman who suffered horrific injuries after being set alight outside her own home.
“Our thoughts very much remain with Brenda and her family as we continue to do everything we can to find out what happened and who is responsible.
“Her family are understandably distraught and have taken the step of releasing her name and photograph to help jog people’s memories around this distressing and highly unusual incident.
“Someone out there knows something. You may have witnessed suspicious activity, heard a conversation, noticed unusual behaviour, or captured something on CCTV or dashcam footage without realising its significance.
“Please do not assume that what you know is too small or unimportant to tell us about. It could be a seemingly insignificant piece of information that provides investigators with the breakthrough they need.
“If you know anything about what happened to Brenda or think you may have information that could assist our inquiries, please come forward. Your information could be crucial in helping us find answers and bring those responsible to justice.”

MPs across factional lines share concerns about policy that legal expert says ‘paints the imprisonment of children as therapeutic’
Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast
Until December last year, Meena Singh was the Victorian commissioner for Aboriginal children and young people, a role that saw her advocating for some of the state’s most vulnerable children.
She had held the role since 2022. In all that time, she says, nobody from the Victorian government had approached her with a proposal like the one the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, announced last week: a $204m “tough love” plan to send children who commit low and mid-level offences to secure facilities, including the former Malmsbury youth justice centre, for schooling, drug and alcohol treatment and life skills.
“If you are on the trajectory of committing crime like carrying a knife or looking to steal cars, you can expect to be detained and be put in this new mandatory detention in Malmsbury,” Carroll told reporters last Sunday.
“We have seen how, where you break the cycle, it can turn young lives around.”
“It is very misleading to try and paint the imprisonment of children as therapeutic,” Singh, now a professor at Monash law school, tells Guardian Australia.
“Children who are getting in trouble with the law, there are reasons behind it … Imprisoning these children is effectively imprisoning them for traumas they have experienced rather than the behaviours they are displaying.”
She is far from alone in her criticism. The Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service called the announcement “mandatory sentencing dressed up as political leadership” and the Justice Reform Initiative said it was a “dramatically disproportionate response”. The same organisations were among the legal and human rights groups that lashed other Labor changes introduced this term in an attempt to bring down the state’s crime rate – including “adult time for violent crime” and tougher bail laws.
Even the state’s union movement has criticised this proposal, with the Trades Hall secretary, Luke Hilakari, taking to his personal social media account to publicly rebuke the government.
“Honestly thought the policy of locking up children for a year for shopping lifting [shoplifting] or vandalism was from the Liberal party,” he wrote, adding that one of the most common items stolen was groceries.
“And if you want to win an election, could we leave issues in the Liberal party frame to the Liberals.”
Hilakari finished his post by sharing a DemosAU poll, released on Monday, showing Labor on a primary vote of 18% – the lowest figure in its history . That same day, Carroll was in South Melbourne spruiking a $70m plan to hire police reservists to reopen police stations Labor has closed over the term and $300m to build and renovate stations.
Half a dozen MPs from across the party’s factional lines, not authorised to speak publicly, also shared their concerns with Guardian Australia. Some said Labor was handing the Liberals a free kick by choosing to campaign on crime after presiding over rising crime rates and the closure of police stations.
Others say they gritted their teeth and supported the earlier measures, hoping it would be enough to stem the bleeding on the issue. This hasn’t eventuated – a separate RedBridge poll, released on Wednesday, had the party at a 23% primary vote. And it said Labor was 18 points behind the Coalition on crime.
Another Labor strategist, who requested anonymity to speak freely, described the announcement as “a metaphor for the complete lack of clarity regarding our identity and message for Victorian voters”.
The strategist was particularly disturbed to see Davydd Griffths, Labor’s candidate in Melbourne – a seat currently held by the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell – standing behind the premier for the press conference.
“What targeted Melbourne voter would support that policy? The focus on crime this week has scrapped any chance of winning Melbourne off the Greens,” they said.
For MPs on the right of the party, it’s “too little too late”. They say crime disproportionately affects working-class communities, particularly in the outer-suburban seats Labor needs to retain – and other MPs would’ve known this earlier if they were actually in touch with their constituents.
“This is a reflection that, since the campaign started three weeks ago, they’ve been copping it out door knocking, at street stalls, shopping centres on crime,” one MP said.
Those on the left say the proposal is further proof Labor has abandoned its values. Carroll has pitched himself as a “centrist”, an “economically conservative, socially progressive premier”. He’s also sought to distance himself from a government he has been part of for more than a decade. The slogan printed on the rear of his big red campaign bus is anything but subtle: “New Premier, New Direction”.
The strategy appears to be based on the idea that voters want a decisive break with the past. But there are concerns that, in trying to disown the government’s record, he is also disowning the Labor movement’s achievements over the past 12 years. It risks giving voters little reason to remember why they voted for them in the first place.
One MP said a growing group of colleagues were “furious” that the new leadership had “overseen the trashing of the government’s legacy and instead delivered an election campaign focused almost exclusively on the Big Build royal commission and law and order – two issues losing votes for Labor”.
“Having lost all but our most rusted-on Labor voters to other parties, it looks like they are now happy to see how far we can push before they leave us as well,” the MP said.
There’s evidence this is happening. Monday’s DemosAU poll had the Greens at a record high 17%. This was prior to Labor’s move to run an open ticket in Prahran , which has angered progressives.
The Greens responded on Friday by confirming they will be running their version of an open ticket – urging people to put the Greens first and One Nation last rather than direct preferences.
There’s no doubt this will hurt Labor in a number of seats, capping off another difficult week on the campaign trail.
Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent. Henry Belot contributed to this reporting

Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows.
The Great British Bake Off presenter said in a statement to the Sun he was "horrified and deeply disturbed" to learn of Brand's crimes, after the disgraced comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault.
Footage of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of Channel 4's Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007 has resurfaced in the aftermath of Brand's conviction.
Fielding described "some of the jokes" he made as "horrible and inappropriate", and said he had not been in contact with Brand "for many years".
"I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand's crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice," Fielding said.
"I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years.
"Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them."
Ross has also released a statement distancing himself from the remarks, saying that his "thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."
Among the resurfaced footage is a clip of Brand and Fielding laughing on an episode of The Russell Brand Show, which aired on BBC Radio 2 in 2007. In it, Brand joked about kissing and holding an underage grasshopper.
"How do you even know if it's a child or an adult? You don't even care, do you," Fielding responded.
Brand can be heard replying: "It's a mistake I've made. I've had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I'm in it, right, I'm kissing it, I'm holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: 'I'm 12.'"
Brand and Fielding also performed charity gigs together as The Goth Detectives.
Fielding said he was "appalled" by some of the jokes he had made alongside Brand
Brand was jailed for 10 and a half years for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others.
Further allegations against him have been made in recent days. More women have made allegations about him in interviews with the Times and a Netflix documentary.
The Times said it could not publish the investigation until the criminal case ended. Brand has denied non-consensual sexual activity.
Police have said Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women.

Andrew McLachlan says he chooses ‘real forests over virtual ones’ as he urges Labor government to consider AI’s impact on artists and environment
Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast
Outspoken Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan has raised the alarm about the approach of his party and the Labor government to AI, urging artists’ copyright not be “sacrificed” for investment and that building new datacentres must not be prioritised above environmental concerns.
As Labor considers copyright changes in an AI policy suite including datacentres, online safety, energy resources and economic benefits, the South Australian backbencher added weight to mooted constitutional challenges as to whether watering down copyright law would be an illegal acquisition of property .
“The works [artists] create must not be sacrificed on the altar of global corporate profiteering,” he said.
“Artists’ property rights must be respected and protected. It is unimaginable that as a nation we might value the machine over beauty created by the artist”.
Although the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has previously declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, some AI companies have rejected making agreements under existing copyright laws, arguing it is too difficult.
AI companies have said they need legal certainty on the copyright issue before investing in Australia, with Anthropic putting foward an “opt out” model which would allow it to scrape music, books and journalism unless a rights holder signals an objection.
Leading voices in the recording industry have raised alarm about any changes to weaken existing copyright law .
McLachlan said the work of artists “nourishes the soul of our nation”, and demanded art be prioritised over the demands of big tech.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
“The principle of fair pay for a fair day’s work must not be forgotten in the age of social media platforms, datacentres and artificial intelligence. AI provides amazing opportunities for our nation. If there are trade-offs then the costs must be clearly articulated and understood.”
Labor and the Coalition have largely agreed on AI-related issues; senator David Pocock has complained about a major party “stitch-up” on AI regulation. This week, the shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, and the shadow cybersecurity minister, Aaron Violi, said in a statement that AI was “too important to become an unnecessarily partisan political contest”, saying they’d “engage constructively” to ensure an “enduring and multipartisan approach” to the technology.
But fellow Coalition members Ross Cadell and Michaelia Cash have backed concerns raised by Aria that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government; the constitutional imperative that the government must acquire property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern in the copyright debate.
McLachlan said any potential compensation arrangements must be considered on an individual basis for each artist, adding it would be difficult to ensure an industry-wide scheme would be fair.
“As a Liberal, I believe property rights are foundational to a healthy democracy and a strong economy,” he said.
“The state should never seek to compulsorily acquire or trade away an individual’s property rights except in very limited circumstances and not without just compensation.”
Labor and the Coalition are both in favour of attracting more AI investment and datacentres to Australia, but the opposition has warned the government against “selling out” Australian rights holders in a rush to secure investment.
The growth of datacentres in Australia is expected to increase emissions and power costs for households, prompting backlash from environmental groups and some communities.
McLachlan, who has spoken strongly on conservation and environmental issues, said: “Datacentres must not be built at the expense of our biodiversity.
“We must explore ways to build sovereign AI capability in a sustainable way.
Earlier this week, Labor announced it will set up a new AI safety regulator and implement six key obligations on AI companies after a breach of government sites by OpenAI.
Labor’s AI package is expected to be unveiled before the end of the year.

Bonnie Tyler died aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year
Bonnie Tyler sings of "love, light and peace" and remembers "the ones who still live on inside our hearts" on her posthumous Christmas single, which was released on Friday.
The popular Welsh powerhouse singer, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year.
Fans were able to hear the Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's husky tones one more time on the festive track titled "Love, Light and Peace".
The last song Tyler recorded features sleigh bells and angels and an ad-libbed farewell: "To all, goodnight."
The lyrics about grief and loss take on new meaning following her death.
Tyler sings: "Blessed are the ones who still live on inside our hearts.
The song was written by Chrissie Hammond and Grammy-winner Terry Britten, who played guitar on Tyler's debut album, The World Starts Tonight in 1977.
Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer for the last song she recorded.
Tyler had "no big ideas" about recording until she was spotted by a talent scout
Tyler's husband of more than 50 years, Robert Sullivan, previously said she would have wanted fans to hear the music she was working on, and gave his blessing for the song's release .
Tyler was born in a Neath council house where she grew up with a love of music before being discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.
After finding fame she was dubbed "the female Rod Stewart" for her husky vocals, and launched a career that spanned 50 years .
In August, fans travelled to Swansea to line the streets as a celebration of life service was held for her at Swansea Minster.

The UN climate chief has warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.
The United Nations' top climate official urged negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey to "avoid tactical delays" that would prevent a deal to stop global warming.
Delegates from more than 200 nations are gathered in the Mediterranean city of Antalya with the core goal of preventing the planet from warming by 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit).
Downtown, thousands of civil society and environmental activists from around the world protested against the consequences of climate change .
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), said getting an agreement is "tough but vital work."
"There ​is no collective success without compromise from every party," he added.
"As we head into the second week, ​I urge ‌parties to move swiftly to the hardest issues and to avoid tactical delays."
Meanwhile, tens of thousands of protesters marched through Antalya on Saturday for climate protection and human rights, according to organizers.
Many were dismayed at the lack of progress and how the climate crisis is taking a back seat.
"The pursuit of profit at all costs continues to set the [global] agenda [and] govern the trajectory of our world, so there is a need to push back," environmental activist Zaki Mamdoo from South Africa told DW.
Luisa Nebauer, the main organizer of Germany's Fridays for Future movement, lamented that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was absent from the conference, along with several other European leaders.
"We won't have a chance to solve any of the crises as long as our planet is destabilizing by the hour," Nebauer told DW. "We must show up!"
Turkish authorities permitted the rally to go ahead, in a country that often bans large public gatherings.
Alongside the march, a parallel "People's Climate Summit" involving hundreds of domestic and international civil society groups takes place in Antalya this weekend.
With inflation, wars, deindustrialization and debt being seen as bigger immediate threats, many governments are watering down their commitments to the clean energy transition, along with the billions required to help developing nations to adapt.
The United ⁠States has snubbed the talks ​for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.
Delegates also face pressure from large fossil-fuel-producing nations to avoid setting stricter targets for a faster phaseout of oil and gas.
Climate advocates in Antalya are growing increasingly frustrated by the lack of commitment and delaying tactics preventing an ambitious deal.
COP31 is seeking to unlock finance and investment , reduce the use of so-called super-pollutants and methane and ensure food security.
Host Turkey is, meanwhile, pushing a plan to expand global electrification. Yet, some environmental groups are disappointed the proposal doesn't push increased electricity use from renewable sources.
A UN report last month warned that, within a few years, the world is set to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming.
The figure, set at COP21 in 2015, is the threshold beyond which most scientists believe the world will see increasingly extreme effects of climate change.
A first draft of a deal text is expected to emerge next week, according to Australia's ​COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.

Kurmaca, belgesel ve animasyon olmak üzere 3 kategoride dünyanın dört bir yanından yüzlerce eserin başvurduğu yarışmada jüri değerlendirmesinin ardından finale kalan 10 güçlü yapımı sinemaseverlerle buluşturuyor.

Country music superstar Garth Brooks will perform a multi-city tour of Ireland in 2027
Fans of Garth Brooks will be brushing off their Stetsons and polishing their cowboy boots after the country music superstar announced he will be performing in multiple cities across Ireland in 2027.
The tour includes Belfast, Galway, Kilkenny, Limerick and Cork and will be the first time he has played in Northern Ireland since his King's Hall gig in November 1998.
The singer has said in the past that Ireland is his favourite place in the world to sing , and the love appears to be mutual as his first two Belfast concerts sold out, with an extra date already added.
So why has an American country music star remained so popular with Irish fans for so many years?
Cathy O'Reilly previously saw Garth Brooks live at two of his Dublin concerts in 2022
Cathy O'Reilly, who is originally from County Monaghan but lives in Belfast, managed to get her tickets for the very first show of Garth Brooks' tour on 21 May 2027 at Boucher Road Playing Fields.
She has already seen Brooks perform live before - twice during his run of concerts in Dublin in 2022 and her love of his music was passed on from her parents and uncles.
"It's growing up listening to him it brings me back to my childhood. My uncle gave me his cd, he didn't even buy me one - just gave me his because I loved him so much."
She believes the Irish link to the US and the fact that fans on the island give the best welcome to performers, are the reasons for Garth Brooks' popularity in Ireland.
"He [Garth Brooks] gives us energy and we're giving it back ten-fold nearly, and we're just so welcoming so he really enjoys coming here."
Peter Aiken, from Aiken Promotions, told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the new Belfast gig is "red hot".
Brooks is the biggest selling artist in US history and is the only artist to pass 200 million albums sold.
In 2014 about 400,000 fans booked tickets to five concerts he had planned for Dublin's Croke Park but Dublin City Council only granted permission for three of them.
Brooks said he would only perform all five concerts or none at all and so the shows were cancelled.
Stephen Butler performs as a Garth Brooks tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls and described his job as "easy" due to the love of Garth Brooks' fans
Stephen Butler from Newtownabbey performs as a Garth Brooks' tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls.
"My mother was a fan when I was younger, she was always playing his music and buying his albums so I loved the songs.
"I knew, with me loving Garth and there being such a following in Ireland, I knew it was the right thing to do."
He went to the Dublin concert in 2022 and while he hasn't yet got tickets for the Ireland dates next year, he hopes to get tickets to at least one of them closer to the time.
Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music"
"I was able to get four or five tickets about a week or two before the Croke Park shows, I'll definitely go - I have to go.
"His band is amazing, he's amazing, and his songs - he's got an endless amount of anthems."
Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music".
"I'm not saying I'm as good as Garth Brooks, but I definitely have his enthusiasm.
"I talk about him and how much I love him throughout the songs and I just identify with them as much as I can.
"My job is easy, I just have to go on there and get everybody singing along with me."
Butler says he thinks the reason Garth Brooks remains so enduringly popular in Ireland is because the people here identify so strongly with his songs.
"Everybody loves Friends In Low Places, people of Ireland love it, they love Callin' Baton Rouge.
"I speak to a lot of people after I play the shows and a lot of people identify with some of the words in the songs, they tell me about a relative that's passed and they seem to have some kind of identification with the songs Tomorrow Never Comes or Unanswered Prayers - it talks about love and about how Garth feels.
"And in amongst Thunder Rolls and the big hits that Garth has, he sings big rocky country rock and ballads, so it's exciting and it's sad - it's an emotional roller coaster," he said.
"And he's such a down-to-earth, genuine, caring person, he seems to be a good soul and I think people people identify with his personality.
"It's a big working-class country and they love someone that's genuine and that talks from the heart."
